facts.statement: Born in Boston on 19 January 1809; died in Baltimore on 7 October 1849.
His parents were actors; after his mother's death in 1811 he grew up with John and Frances Allan in Richmond and spent part of his childhood in Britain.
Attended the University of Virginia in 1826; published Tamerlane and Other Poems and enlisted in the Army in 1827; became sergeant major; attended West Point in 1830–1831 and was court-martialed.
Worked for the Southern Literary Messenger, Burton's Gentleman's Magazine, Graham's Magazine and the Broadway Journal; the last briefly belonged to him.
The Raven appeared in 1845; Wiley and Putnam published the twelve-story Tales in New York that year, including the three Dupin tales and The Fall of the House of Usher.
Virginia Poe died in 1847; Eureka appeared in 1848.

uncertainties.statement: The precise medical cause of Poe's death is not conclusively established; no diagnosis is asserted here.
No military decoration is claimed. West Point attendance and enlisted rank are career facts, not honours.

en.tagline: The calculating mind and the haunted imagination.
en.intro: A cipher on a scrap of parchment, an ancestral house on the edge of collapse, a letter hidden in plain sight: Poe makes the smallest detail carry the weight of a whole story. His tales lead reason and terror into the same room.
en.orientation: Poe's working world was the American magazine: a place for stories, reviews and argument, and a precarious source of income. The poet of The Raven was also an exacting editor. His fiction brings that discipline to extremes of fear, speculation and analytical pursuit.
origin: Born in Boston to actors, Poe lost his mother in early childhood. John and Frances Allan brought him up in Richmond; schooling in Britain and a brief period at the University of Virginia widened the geography of his youth.
career: In 1827, the year of Tamerlane and Other Poems, he enlisted in the United States Army. He rose to sergeant major before leaving for a different course. West Point followed in 1830; court-martial ended his time there in 1831.

Editing took him through the Southern Literary Messenger, Burton's Gentleman's Magazine and Graham's Magazine. In New York he briefly owned the Broadway Journal. The Raven brought fame in 1845; the business of literature remained insecure. Virginia died in 1847, and Eureka appeared the following year.
literature: The twelve tales collected in 1845 hold several kinds of invention together. Dupin follows the relations between facts; the narrator of The Black Cat attempts to account for his own violence; the house of Usher binds landscape, sound and apprehension into a single pressure. The methods differ, but every selected detail matters.
Read in their original order, the stories move between ciphers, catastrophe, speculative dialogue and the crowded city. This is a more various Poe than a gallery of Gothic horrors alone can suggest.
en.legacy: Poe's stories make reading an active contest with appearances. We listen to a voice, weigh its evidence and discover how readily attention can be directed elsewhere. The attraction lies as much in that controlled movement as in the revelation at the end.
en.bridge: The twelve stories of Tales recover the shape of the 1845 collection, with its mysteries, speculative encounters and Gothic interiors.
en.description: Edgar Allan Poe (1809–1849): poet, critic, editor and author of Tales. Explore his life and the AETERNUS English edition, coming 4 November 2026.
